preamble: Backing of the voiced dental fricative [ð] to the voiced velar fricative [ɣ] is the defining change of late Gaelic: Old and Middle Irish lenited d (spelled ḋ/dh) was [ð], but between the 13th and 18th centuries all dental fricatives were lost across the Goidelic languages, broad [ð] merging with lenited g as [ɣ] and slender [ðʲ] with [ʝ]. As a result, Modern Irish and Scottish Gaelic pronounce the spellings dh and gh identically, and lenited d-initial words such as dhá 'two' begin with [ɣ].

examples.from: Old Irish dá 'two', lenited form pronounced with [ð-]
examples.note: The lenited numeral, used attributively before nouns, now begins with the velar fricative; dh and gh are no longer distinguished.
The standalone counting form carries lenition, and its initial dh is pronounced [ɣ], identical to gh.

sources: Wikipedia (2026). Early Modern Irish: Phonology (loss of all dental fricatives, [θ(ʲ), ð(ʲ)] > [h, ɣ(ʲ)]). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Modern_Irish
